whyNot: The **ventromedial** prefrontal cortex is tied to comorbid conduct, oppositional and mood or anxiety symptoms, not to sustaining attention.
The **orbitofrontal** loop is linked to impulsivity such as blurting out, not to trouble finishing tasks.
The **dACC** handles selective attention (focusing, careless mistakes), not sustaining effort over a task.
The supplementary motor area is linked to motor **hyperactivity**, not to difficulty sustaining attention.
q11-01.why: Trouble sustaining attention and solving problems reflects inefficient processing in the **DLPFC**, which the n-back test activates and which underlies executive dysfunction across many disorders.

whyNot: Sustained attention and the DLPFC are probed by the **n-back** test, not by the Stroop task.
Impulsivity maps to the orbitofrontal cortex, and a color-naming Stroop task does not measure it.
Hyperactivity is modulated by the prefrontal motor cortex loop; Stroop tests **selective attention**, not motor activity.
Mood instability is a comorbid symptom tied to the VMPFC, and the Stroop task does not probe it.
q11-02.why: The Stroop task, naming the ink color instead of reading the word, demands **selective attention** and should activate the **dACC**; ADHD patients may under-recruit it or recruit it only with great effort.

whyNot: The **DLPFC** relates to sustained attention and problem solving, not to blurting out and interrupting.
The **cerebellum** is not part of the prefrontal loop the book uses for impulsivity, which runs through the orbitofrontal cortex.
The thalamus is only one stop in the loop; its prefrontal hub for impulsivity is the **orbitofrontal** cortex.
The **hippocampus** is not a region the book assigns to impulsive symptoms of ADHD; the orbitofrontal cortex is.
q11-03.why: Impulsive symptoms such as blurting things out, not waiting a turn and interrupting arise from a cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop centered on the **orbitofrontal cortex**.

whyNot: The book routes the motor loop through the **putamen** (lateral striatum), not through a caudate-only pathway.
The hypothalamus is not part of this cortico-striato-thalamo-cortical loop; the striatal stop is the **putamen**.
The amygdala is not in this circuit; it runs from prefrontal motor cortex to **putamen** to thalamus and back.
The nucleus accumbens is a reward center where phasic DA reinforces learning, not the relay for motor hyperactivity.
q11-04.why: Motor activity is modulated by a loop passing from prefrontal motor cortex through the **putamen** (lateral striatum) and thalamus, then back again.

whyNot: The occipital cortex is not a prefrontal region, and the book ties oppositional comorbidity to the **VMPFC** instead.
The **dACC** is linked to selective attention problems such as careless mistakes, not to tantrums or defiance.
The **DLPFC** governs sustained attention and problem solving, not temper tantrums and aggression.
The supplementary motor area is linked to motor **hyperactivity**, not to oppositional behavior.
q11-05.why: Inadequate tuning of the **ventromedial prefrontal cortex** is hypothesized to produce comorbid conduct, oppositional and mood or anxiety symptoms such as tantrums, argumentativeness and aggression.

whyNot: Naming the ink color of a word is the **Stroop** task, which tests selective attention, not the n-back.
Pressing a button for the number on screen is the **0-back** version, the easiest level.
Delayed list recall is not the n-back as described; it asks for a number seen one step earlier.
Withholding a response to a target is not the n-back design, which asks for the **previous** number.
q11-06.why: In the 0-back the participant reports the number on screen; in the **1-back** the button must match the number seen one step earlier, and a higher n makes the test harder.

whyNot: Receptors of the **α1** type are less sensitive and are recruited only when NE is too high, which impairs working memory.
**D1** receptors respond to dopamine rather than norepinephrine.
**β1** receptors, like α1, are the less sensitive receptors recruited when NE is excessive, harming working memory.
The α2C subtype is densest in striatum with few in the PFC; the prefrontal benefit comes from postsynaptic **α2A**.
q11-07.why: Low to moderate NE preferentially engages the most sensitive postsynaptic **α2A** receptors, strengthening prefrontal signals; too much NE spills onto less sensitive α1 and β1 receptors and impairs function.

whyNot: D4 is not among the prefrontal dopamine receptors the book ranks; its sensitivity order is D3, then D2, then D1.
**D2** is the moderately sensitive receptor, stimulated after D3 but before D1.
**D3** is the most sensitive receptor, recruited first when DA release is low.
D5 is not part of the sensitivity ranking the book gives for prefrontal dopamine receptors.
q11-08.why: D1 is the least sensitive DA receptor and predominates postsynaptically in the PFC, so low DA leaves it under-stimulated; tuning requires DA high enough to reach an **optimal D1** level.

whyNot: **D3** is the most sensitive dopamine receptor and not a norepinephrine target, so it cannot explain the stress effect.
Imidazoline receptors are clonidine targets tied to sedation and hypotension, not to stress-related working-memory loss.
**α2A** is recruited at modest NE and improves prefrontal function; the harm comes from other receptors.
5HT1A is a serotonin receptor, and the book attributes NE-driven working-memory loss to α1 and β1 receptors.
q11-09.why: Too much NE, as in stress, anxiety, substance abuse or mania, swamps the synapse and also stimulates the less sensitive **α1 and β1** receptors, which impairs working memory.

whyNot: Phasic firing is normal; DA neurons burst when salient inputs arrive, so it is present in healthy people.
A steady baseline tone in the PFC is **tonic** firing, the opposite of phasic bursts.
Phasic firing is a property of dopamine neurons, not a purely noradrenergic process.
Phasic bursts recruit **all** three DA receptor subtypes, not D3 alone.
Blocking NMDA receptors is not how the book explains α2A signal strengthening, which runs through Gi, cAMP and HCN channels.
Opening chloride channels is not the mechanism; α2A works through cAMP and HCN channel **closure**.
NE does not change HCN channel expression; it closes the existing channels by lowering cAMP.
A Gs-driven cAMP rise that opens HCN channels describes **D1** signaling, which leaks the signal.
q11-11.why: α2A receptors couple to **Gi**, which lowers cAMP and closes HCN channels, so the incoming signal is not shunted out of the spine and survives to strengthen network connectivity.

whyNot: D1 acts through Gs-linked cAMP and HCN channels, not by directly depolarizing via sodium channels.
Lowering cAMP and closing HCN channels is the **α2A**/NE action, the opposite of D1.
D1 is Gs-linked and **raises** cAMP, so it clearly does affect cAMP.
Postsynaptic D1 receptors predominate in the prefrontal cortex, so D1 does not act only **presynaptically**.
q11-12.why: D1 receptors are Gs-linked, so dopamine raises cAMP, which opens HCN channels and lowers membrane resistance. Moderate D1 stimulation reduces noise, but excessive stimulation lets the signal leak away.

whyNot: Phasic bursts describe how dopamine neurons fire, not what open HCN channels do to a spine's input.
Nothing in the HCN mechanism sends signals back to the locus coeruleus, which is the source of NE input.
Amplification happens when HCN channels are **closed**, as with α2A stimulation.
The signal is not unchanged; an open channel lowers membrane resistance and the input is lost.
q11-13.why: Open HCN channels lower membrane resistance, so incoming signals are **shunted out** of the spine and lost, whereas closed channels let the signal survive and travel on.

whyNot: Increased signal with reduced noise is the **optimal** tuned state, not the low NE plus low DA state.
Low NE does reduce the signal, but low DA **increases** rather than reduces noise.
Output is not unchanged; the mistuned neuron yields a poor signal-to-noise ratio causing inattention or hyperactivity.
Low NE **decreases** the signal rather than increasing it, so this choice has both effects backward.
q11-14.why: Low NE means too little α2A stimulation, so the signal weakens; low DA means too little D1 stimulation, so noise rises. Together they give the poor signal-to-noise ratio of untreated ADHD.

whyNot: 25% understates it; the book places ADHD heritability at roughly three-quarters.
95% overstates it; genetic causation is strong but complex and multifactorial, about 75%.
10% is far too low for a disorder with such a large genetic contribution.
40% is too low; the book gives about 75% for ADHD.
q11-15.why: Genetic influence on ADHD is among the largest in psychiatry, roughly **75%**, though many genes contribute and causation is complex, with delayed prefrontal maturation as a unifying idea.

whyNot: Age 18 is not the cutoff; the criteria demand a childhood onset, by 12.
Age 5 is too early; DSM-5 allows onset up to 12, and preschool inattention is hard to recognize.
Age 7 was the older **DSM-IV** cutoff, which DSM-5 extended.
Age 16 is not a cutoff the book cites; the current limit is **12**.
q11-16.why: Onset before age **12** is the DSM-5 requirement, loosened from age 7 in DSM-IV; experts still debate whether late-onset adult ADHD should be excluded.

whyNot: Motor hyperactivity declines notably by adolescence and early adulthood.
Climbing and running are overt hyperactive behaviors, which fade rather than persist.
Impulsivity also **declines** by adolescence and early adulthood.
Leaving one's seat is another hyperactive symptom that wanes with age.
About half is the figure for **children and adolescents** diagnosed and treated, not adults.
One-third is not the book's number, and the stem asks about adults; about half of children are treated.
Three-quarters is the heritability estimate, not the fraction of adults diagnosed and treated.
Nearly all is wrong; adult ADHD is largely unrecognized and untreated.
q11-18.why: About half of children and adolescents are diagnosed and treated, but fewer than **1 in 5** adults, since retrospective diagnosis of onset before 12 is hard and symptoms often go untreated.

whyNot: In adults ADHD is often an afterthought, addressed once the substance, mood and anxiety problems are managed.
Nicotine dependence is addressed eventually, after cognitive symptoms are under control, not first.
Giving a stimulant to someone actively abusing drugs is poorly advised; a tonic NET or α2A agent is preferred.
Anxiety disorders are treated after substance abuse in this scheme, since continued use blocks progress.
q11-19.why: In complex cases little progress is possible while the patient keeps abusing alcohol or stimulants, so **substance abuse** is usually stabilized first, with ADHD fine-tuned afterward.

whyNot: The rate is similar to that of schizophrenia, not half of it.
Smoking is more common than in the general population, not the same, perhaps because nicotine eases untreated ADHD symptoms.
Ten times overshoots; the book gives about **double** the US rate.
Half the general rate is the opposite direction; smoking is twice as frequent.
q11-20.why: Adults and adolescents with ADHD smoke about **twice** as often as the general US population, similar to patients with schizophrenia, perhaps because nicotine releases dopamine and boosts arousal.

whyNot: Blocking D2 receptors is how tics would be treated, not why a stimulant worsens them.
Excess cortical NE is not offered as the reason; the conflict is a DA mismatch between motor striatum and cortex.
Low striatal DA is backwards; tics represent hypothetically **excess** DA in the motor striatum.
α2A overstimulation is not cited; tics worsen because stimulants add to already high motor-striatal DA.
q11-21.why: Tics reflect hypothetically excessive DA activity in the motor striatum, while ADHD reflects deficient cortical DA; a stimulant that fixes the cortex can push striatal DA higher and worsen tics.

whyNot: Inhibiting VMAT2 is an amphetamine property; methylphenidate has no action at VMAT2.
DAT reversal occurs with high-dose **amphetamine**, not with methylphenidate.
Competitive pseudosubstrate action is amphetamine's mode; methylphenidate binds a distinct, **allosteric** site.
Displacing DA from vesicles is amphetamine's action after it is carried into the neuron; methylphenidate never enters.
q11-22.why: Methylphenidate binds DAT and NET at a site distinct from the monoamine site, so it stops the pumps without being transported inside or touching VMAT2, unlike amphetamine.

whyNot: Both isomers bind NET and DAT; the **D**-isomer is simply much more potent.
Potency is not equal; the D-isomer far exceeds L at both transporters.
The racemate is active mainly through its D-isomer, and D-methylphenidate is also sold alone.
The **L**-isomer is the weaker one at both NET and DAT.
q11-23.why: Both enantiomers bind NET and DAT, but **D-methylphenidate** is much more potent than L at both, which is why D-methylphenidate is also marketed on its own.

whyNot: Daytrana is a patch worn in the morning, with a single peak at 7 to 10 hours.
Focalin is immediate-release D-methylphenidate, with an early peak and a second dose at lunch.
Ritalin LA is a morning capsule with two strong peaks, early and at about 4 hours.
Concerta is a morning tablet with a small early peak and a 12-hour duration.
q11-24.why: **Jornay PM** is taken in the evening, with initial absorption delayed about 10 hours and a single peak near 14 hours, so drug levels are already present as the patient wakes.

whyNot: Quillivant XR is a suspension with a single peak at about 5 hours and a 12-hour duration.
Concerta has a small early peak and lasts 12 hours, not two strong peaks.
Cotempla XR-ODT is listed as a 12-hour once-daily tablet, with no two-peak profile.
Immediate-release Ritalin gives one early peak lasting 3 to 4 hours.
q11-25.why: **Ritalin LA** is a capsule built for two strong peaks, one early and one near 4 hours, covering a 6 to 8 hour duration, whereas the other products listed have a single peak or a different profile.

whyNot: Direct D1 stimulation is a postsynaptic effect; amphetamine's flood comes from vesicle displacement and DAT reversal.
Allosteric DAT blockade is **methylphenidate's** mechanism, not amphetamine's.
COMT inhibition is not part of the amphetamine mechanism the book describes.
Blocking α2 autoreceptors is not how amphetamine floods DA; it enters terminals and displaces DA.
q11-26.why: At abuse doses amphetamine is carried into the terminal and then into vesicles via VMAT2, displacing DA; rising cytoplasmic DA reverses DATs and opens channels, dumping DA into the synapse.

whyNot: Only DAT action is wrong; mixed salts also act on NET, with relatively **more** NET action than D-amphetamine.
Less NET action reverses it; the L-isomer is about as potent as D at NET.
VMAT effects remain; both D,L and D amphetamine are competitive inhibitors at VMAT.
Only NET action is wrong; both preparations still act more on DAT than on NET.
q11-27.why: The L-isomer is about as potent as D at NET but weaker at DAT, so mixed D,L salts add relative NET action versus D-amphetamine alone, though DAT action still exceeds NET action.

whyNot: It is amphetamine-based and linked to lysine, so it is not a **methylphenidate** prodrug.
Transdermal delivery describes a methylphenidate patch; lisdexamfetamine is an oral capsule.
It is a prodrug needing cleavage, not a direct α2A agonist; those are guanfacine and clonidine.
Racemic D,L salts are a different product class; lisdexamfetamine contains only the **D**-isomer.
q11-28.why: Lisdexamfetamine is D-amphetamine linked to lysine; it is inactive until cleaved in the stomach and is then absorbed slowly, giving the gradual delivery of a slow-dose stimulant.

whyNot: Adderall XR is listed at 8 to 12 hours.
Dexedrine capsules are listed at 6 to 8 hours.
Evekeo is an immediate-release tablet lasting about 6 hours.
Zenzedi is an immediate-release tablet lasting 4 to 5 hours.
q11-29.why: **Mydayis** is an extended-release mixed amphetamine salt capsule listed at up to 16 hours, the longest duration in the tables, and is approved from age 13 upward.

whyNot: Occupancy of 20 to 30% falls below the likely 50 to 60% threshold, so benefit would not begin.
Complete blockade is not required; sudden, complete DAT blockade is the catastrophic, abuse-linked pattern.
80 to 90% overshoots the threshold; rapid, high occupancy raises abuse risk rather than being needed.
5 to 10% is far too little occupancy to reach the therapeutic threshold.
q11-30.why: ADHD benefit begins only once DAT occupancy rises above a critical threshold, probably around **50 to 60%**, and stops as soon as occupancy falls back below it, much like hypnotic onset and offset.

whyNot: Hallucinations are not linked to continuous DAT engagement; the book ties it to delayed antidepressant effects.
Immediate ADHD benefit comes from crossing an occupancy **threshold**, not from weeks of continuous engagement.
Rapid tolerance is not discussed; the weeks-long consequence is delayed downstream molecular change.
Immediate euphoria arises from fast, high occupancy, not slow, continuous engagement.
q11-31.why: Antidepressant effects of DAT or NET engagement need round-the-clock occupancy for weeks to trigger downstream events like neurotrophic factor production; the immediate DA rise is not antidepressant.

whyNot: **Rebound** is the opposite problem: levels drop too early in the evening, bringing hyperactivity and insomnia.
Too short an action causes late-afternoon and evening symptoms, not excess focus with sleeplessness.
Delayed onset produces **morning** symptoms, not evening insomnia.
The model explains insomnia by DAT occupancy staying above threshold too long, not by NET occupancy.
q11-32.why: If DAT blockade stays above the therapeutic threshold too long into the evening, benefit continues but late-day side effects, notably **insomnia**, appear; the dose should drop below threshold by bedtime.

whyNot: Sensitization is not the term the book uses for falling evening levels; it names this pattern rebound.
Tachyphylaxis is not the book's term here; the evening pattern of early level decline is rebound.
Withdrawal psychosis is not described; the book calls evening hyperactivity and insomnia from falling levels rebound.
Tolerance would mean a shrinking effect over time, while this scenario is about levels falling too early in the day.
q11-33.why: **Rebound** occurs when evening serum levels fall too early after the day's dose, so DAT occupancy drops below threshold and the patient becomes hyperactive and cannot sleep.

whyNot: Swallowed IR drug reaches the brain more slowly than snorted, injected or smoked drug.
Transdermal delivery is a slow-dose route giving gradual, steady levels, the opposite of fastest entry.
Oral extended-release is built for gradual, sustained delivery, not rapid entry.
Intranasal is faster than oral but slower than intravenous and smoking.
q11-34.why: Brain entry speed rises from oral to intranasal to intravenous to **smoked**, and the quicker and fuller the DAT blockade, the greater the reinforcement and abuse liability.

whyNot: The mechanism still involves NET and DAT, not serotonin; stimulants here are norepinephrine and dopamine reuptake blockers.
Slow-dose preparations are absorbed orally; their lower abuse potential comes from delivery speed.
Slow-dose stimulants block transporters rather than D2 receptors; accumbens D2 signaling is simply not driven up.
They do bind DAT, but not quickly or extensively enough in the accumbens to raise phasic signaling.
Lisdexamfetamine is a prodrug absorbed slowly and counts among the slow-dose stimulants.
Transdermal methylphenidate is a **slow-dose** formulation.
Extended-release D-methylphenidate is listed as slow-dose.
OROS methylphenidate is a slow-dose product with gradually rising levels.
q11-36.why: Immediate-release oral stimulants, like intravenous, smoked or snorted ones, produce a rapid rise in NE and DA and count as pulsatile, while extended-release forms and the prodrug are slow-dose.

whyNot: Brief high peaks are **pulsatile** delivery, linked to abuse and euphoria rather than therapeutic benefit.
Maximal phasic DA release is not the goal; the aim is mainly tonic firing with only judicious phasic increase.
DAT-only effects at high doses ignore NET; the best use targets both transporters rather than raising the dose.
Rapid, complete DAT blockade is the catastrophic pattern associated with abuse.
q11-37.why: The ideal is slow onset, robust but sub-saturating NET and DAT occupancy, and a long duration, giving hours of ADHD relief without euphoria.

whyNot: D1 agonism is not atomoxetine's action; it is a NET inhibitor that indirectly lets DA act on D1.
MAO-B inhibition is not part of atomoxetine's action in the book.
Atomoxetine does not release DA from vesicles; it blocks reuptake.
DATs are scarce in the prefrontal cortex, so DAT blockade is not how DA rises there.
q11-38.why: In the prefrontal cortex DATs are scarce, so NETs inactivate much of the DA as well as NE; blocking NETs with atomoxetine therefore raises both NE and DA there.

whyNot: D2 blockade is an antipsychotic-type action and plays no role here; atomoxetine works at NET.
Being a prodrug is not the book's reason; the explanation is regional, few NETs in the accumbens.
It does reach the brain, raising prefrontal NE and DA; the low abuse potential is explained by the accumbens.
α2A agonism characterizes guanfacine and clonidine, not atomoxetine, which is a NET inhibitor.
q11-39.why: The nucleus accumbens has few NE neurons and NETs, so NET inhibition raises neither NE nor DA there; without that reward-center effect, atomoxetine is thought to lack reinforcing or addictive potential.

whyNot: NRIs are not always inferior; for stimulant-naive patients and after longer treatment they may do as well.
Atomoxetine is approved for both children and adults.
Plasma-level dependence is typical of stimulants; NRIs give round-the-clock relief.
Larger short-term effect sizes belong to stimulants; NRIs are generally smaller in short-term trials.
Bupropion is a weak NRI and weak DAT inhibitor (NDRI), not the well-investigated approved agent.
Reboxetine is listed as an NRI among NET inhibitors, but the book does not describe it as approved for ADHD.
Desipramine is a TCA with notable NRI action that has been tried in ADHD, but it is not the approved agent.
Nortriptyline is likewise a TCA with NRI action used with varying success, not an approved ADHD drug.
q11-41.why: Several agents with NRI properties (bupropion, desipramine, nortriptyline) have been tried in ADHD with varying success, but only **atomoxetine** is well investigated and approved.

whyNot: Guanfacine is not more sedating; it is about 10 times weaker than clonidine at causing sedation.
Imidazoline binding is a **clonidine** property, which guanfacine lacks.
Guanfacine is an agonist at α2A, not a blocker of those receptors.
Only the controlled-release guanfacine is approved for ADHD, not an immediate-release form.
β1 is a beta-adrenergic receptor recruited when NE is excessive, not an α2 subtype.
α2A is the dominant prefrontal subtype for NE's beneficial effects, not the thalamic sedative one.
α2C receptors are densest in striatum, not thalamus.
α1D is an α1 subtype that opposes α2 actions at high NE, not the thalamic sedation receptor.
q11-43.why: **α2B** receptors are concentrated in the thalamus and may mediate the sedating actions of NE, which helps explain the sedation seen with less selective α2 agonists.

whyNot: Working-memory gains come from α2A stimulation in the PFC, not from imidazoline receptors.
Tic exacerbation is not attributed to imidazoline binding; clonidine is used off-label for Tourette syndrome.
Weight gain is not attributed to imidazoline receptor binding in the book.
Abuse potential is absent for these agents, which lack action at postsynaptic DA receptors.
q11-44.why: Clonidine, unlike guanfacine, also binds imidazoline receptors, which are thought to account for part of its sedating and blood-pressure-lowering effects.

whyNot: Accumbens DA is not the issue; the stimulant already optimized DA and reduced the noise.
D2 blockade is not guanfacine's mechanism; it stimulates postsynaptic α2A receptors.
The stimulant did not raise NE too much; NE stays very low in the VMPFC.
Lowering serotonin is not the rationale; the target is the NE signal via α2A.
q11-45.why: The stimulant fixes DA and reduces noise but leaves very low NE in the VMPFC, so the signal stays weak; guanfacine ER stimulates α2A receptors to restore it and may help oppositional behavior.

whyNot: Neither is a **controlled substance**: acting at α2 receptors rather than DA receptors, they carry no abuse potential.
Both act at α2 receptors, not mainly DA receptors.
Both are used off-label for **Tourette** syndrome, among other conditions.
Only controlled-release clonidine is approved for ADHD; clonidine otherwise treats hypertension.
H3 antagonism is a wake-promoting mechanism from the sleep chapter, not viloxazine's.
An α2A agonist describes guanfacine or clonidine, while viloxazine is a **NET** inhibitor.
A DAT inhibitor once approved for appetite suppression describes **mazindol**, a different agent in testing.
A triple reuptake inhibitor describes **centanafadine**, not viloxazine.
q11-47.why: Viloxazine ER is a selective NRI, once marketed abroad for depression, with added 5HT2B and 5HT2C actions; mazindol (DAT) and centanafadine (triple) are other future agents.

whyNot: ADHD can be treated alongside anxiety; the book recommends augmenting rather than withholding treatment.
Cocaine-like DAT blockade carries abuse liability, and stimulants risk worsening anxiety.
A benzodiazepine-stimulant combination is not suggested; the book favors tonic activators over stimulants here.
Immediate-release amphetamine is a pulsatile stimulant that may worsen anxiety and is increasingly avoided.
q11-48.why: Stimulants may worsen anxiety, so the book suggests augmenting anxiolytic or antidepressant therapy with a long-acting NET inhibitor or α2A agonist, which are tonic activators without abuse potential.

whyNot: Blocking prefrontal D1 receptors is backwards; the rationale is to **stimulate** them.
α2A activation is guanfacine's role, not the serotonin-dopamine antagonist's.
Raising accumbens DA contradicts the aim of reducing limbic DA activity at **D2** receptors.
NET inhibition belongs to atomoxetine, not to the serotonin-dopamine antagonist's rationale.
Phasic-only firing is not described; the progression is from high to depleted levels.
Levels do not normalize on their own; poor signal persists until treatment optimizes them.
The book describes no switch to serotonin; NE and DA simply become depleted.
Rising further indefinitely is wrong; levels plummet through depletion over time.
q11-50.why: With chronic stress, NE and DA first surge, worsening signal and noise, then plummet from depletion with no relief in signal output; treatment aims to raise both to optimal.
